name: createContext()
desc: Creates a named channel. The argument is only used when no provider exists above the consumer.

name: <Ctx.Provider value>
desc: Publishes a value to every consumer below it. The nearest provider wins.

name: useContext()
desc: Reads the nearest provider value. The component re-renders when that value changes.
body:
There is no selector. A component that reads `{ user, cart }` re-renders when either one changes, even if it only displays the cart.

The hook must be called at the top level, never inside a condition, a loop, or a callback.

name: context custom hook
syntax: function useThing() { const v = useContext(Ctx); if (!v) throw new Error(...); return v; }
desc: Wraps useContext with a guard and a readable name. Keeps the context object private to its file.

name: split state and actions
syntax:
const StateCtx = createContext(null);
const ActionsCtx = createContext(null);
desc: Two contexts instead of one object: readers subscribe to state, writers get a value that never changes.
body:
A component that only calls `add` reads the actions context and never re-renders when the list changes. That is the cheapest performance fix available in a context-heavy tree, and it costs one extra `createContext` line.

Split further only when a real problem shows: a large list where only the count is displayed, for example.

name: default value
desc: The fallback only applies when no provider is above the consumer. It is not state and never changes.
body: `createContext()` with no argument gives `undefined`, and the failure appears later as a destructuring error that does not mention context. Either pass a usable fallback or pass `null` and guard in a custom hook.

name: nested providers
desc: The nearest provider wins for everything inside it. Nesting is legal and useful for a modal or a preview pane.
body: An accidental second provider is a silent override: the outer value is simply ignored below it. When a component shows the wrong value, walk up the tree and count the providers before changing any state.

name: memoized provider value
syntax: const value = useMemo(() => ({ a, b }), [a, b]);
desc: Keeps the provider value identical between renders so consumers do not re-render for nothing.
body: Memoizing the object is not enough if a field inside it is unstable. A plain `toggle` function is recreated on every render, so the memoized object still changes. Wrap the function in `useCallback` first, then the object.

name: React.memo
desc: Skips a re-render when every prop is equal by Object.is. One level deep only.
body: A new object, array, or arrow function from the parent fails the comparison, so `memo` is common and often useless. It also does not block re-renders caused by the component's own state, or by a context it reads.

name: memo with compare
desc: Custom comparison. Return true when the props count as equal, which skips the render.
body: The return value is inverted compared with `shouldComponentUpdate`: `true` means equal, so no render. Keep the comparison cheap and make sure every prop the component reads is covered, or it will show stale data.

name: useMemo
syntax: const value = useMemo(() => compute(a, b), [a, b]);
desc: Caches the result of a calculation until a dependency changes. The function must be pure.

name: useCallback
desc: Returns the same function object while the dependencies are equal. Needed for memoized children and dependency arrays.
body:
`useCallback(fn, deps)` is `useMemo(() => fn, deps)`. It does not make the function faster and it is pointless for a handler used only on a DOM element.

```jsx
// No benefit here, nobody compares this function
<button onClick={() => setOpen(true)}>Open</button>
```

name: stable callback with updater
desc: Reads the previous state through the updater instead of closing over the current value, so the array can stay empty.
body: This is the cheapest way to keep a handler stable and correct at the same time. The moment the callback reads a state value directly, that value belongs in the dependency array, and the stable identity is gone.

name: dependency array
syntax: useMemo(fn, [a, b]); // every value read goes here
desc: Compared element by element with Object.is. List every prop, state, and local function the callback reads.
body:
An empty array means compute once. A missing array means compute on every render. Module-level imports and `setState` functions from `useState` are stable and can be left out.

Do not silence the lint warning by deleting a dependency. The bug shows up later as data that stops updating.

name: stale closure
syntax: useEffect(() => { ... }, []); // captures the first render's values
desc: A function with an empty dependency array keeps reading the values from the render that created it.

name: memo and children
desc: children is a prop. A new element on every parent render makes the memo comparison fail.
body: The usual fix is structural: move the state that changes into the smallest component that needs it, so the expensive subtree is not a child of the thing that re-renders.
